source.title: Learning Video Representations from Large Language Models
source.authors: Yue Zhao; Ishan Misra; Philipp Krahenbuhl; Rohit Girdhar

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether downstream video-task performance improves with increased training data and model size, using downstream metrics rather than language-model held-out loss.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws, test extrapolation from small runs, or examine compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Its relevant results are downstream video-task metrics across training-data amounts and model-size settings. Other downstream benchmark results without a scale comparison do not bear on the listed claim versions.
record.test_reason: This is a video-language method paper (LaViLa). Its 'scaling' results are qualitative: its method beats a ground-truth-only baseline at four narration fractions, and gains grow with a larger NARRATOR video encoder (Table 7c). It measures no pretraining loss, fits no power law and tests no extrapolation or allocation. It reports no predictable relation between scale or loss and downstream performance. The study does not test any version of the scaling-law claim.
record.authors_conclusion: Roughly right. The authors say LaViLa shows positive scaling behaviour with more narrations, larger visual backbones and stronger LLMs. This is a qualitative claim about their method's gains over baselines, not a fitted scaling law.
record.recipe_differences: This is video-language representation learning, not a language-model held-out-loss scaling-law study. It varies annotated-video data and video-encoder size and reports downstream task scores, without fitting loss laws or testing compute-optimal allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Downstream performance changes with the fraction of available narrations and with encoder size; the text reports larger gains when more data is available and steadily increasing retrieval performance as NARRATOR's video encoder is strengthened.

fits_no_version.finding: In video-language contrastive pretraining, LaViLa's zero-shot gains over a ground-truth baseline grow with narration fraction (10–100%). EK-100 MIR zero-shot mAP also rises with a larger NARRATOR video encoder and with the TSF-L vs TSF-B dual encoder.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: LLM-generated pseudo-narration gains for video representation learning grow with data and model size (qualitative, method-specific).

record.problems: The scale-related numerical results are presented in figures and their values cannot be assigned reliably from the flattened text; no uncertainty estimates are reported. The experiments cover selected video tasks and settings, not held-out language-model loss or a fitted general scaling law.
record.rows_left_out: No other scale-related results were left out. Other benchmark comparisons and ablations do not measure the claim's scale-related downstream behavior.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss vs parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from fitted small runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No predictable downstream-vs-scale or downstream-vs-loss relation. There are only a few qualitative method ablations.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's 'tests/T2' and V6 'supports' labels are overturned. The rows compare the study's own method with baselines or are component ablations of very few points, with no scaling relation. The scaling statements are qualitative and untested against any functional form.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out language-model pretraining loss or power-law fit in parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of larger-run loss from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or fitted parameter/token scaling exponents.
No comparison of depth, width, or other architecture details at fixed parameter count and loss.
The paper studies video representations, but does not test whether the same held-out-loss power-law form holds in video or another modality.
Tests downstream video-task performance against training-data amount and model-size settings; does not test prediction from pretraining loss or fit a general quantitative scaling relation.
No comparison of fitted exponents, fitting choices, or departures from a single power law.
